In today’s decree, he appointed Mohsen Rezaei as his representative to the Supreme National Security Council, praising his role in the Iran-Iraq War and thanking outgoing official Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr. A separate government announcement says President Pezeshkian also appointed Rezaei as council secretary following Zolghadr’s resignation. Rezaei commanded the IRGC from 1981 to 1997 and has taken a hard line on Hormuz, negotiations and military retaliation. This looks less like an ordinary reshuffle and more like further concentration of security policy in veteran IRGC hands.

RT by @hey_itsmyturn: 🇺🇸 Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says pipelines could divert 50–70% of Hormuz energy traffic within two years, making the strait almost “irrelevant.” Existing bypasses: • Saudi East–West pipeline: Persian Gulf fields → Yanbu on the Red Sea, rated at 7 million barrels/day. Actual exports are constrained by refineries, storage and Yanbu’s loading terminals. • UAE Habshan–Fujairah pipeline: Abu Dhabi → Gulf of Oman, about 1.8 million bpd. A second line planned for 2027 could raise combined capacity to roughly 3.6 million. • Iran’s Goreh–Jask pipeline: Iranian fields → Gulf of Oman, but effective capacity is only about 300,000 bpd. • Iraq–Türkiye pipeline: Kirkuk → Ceyhan, currently carrying a fraction of its 1.5 million-bpd theoretical capacity. Extending it to southern Iraq remains a proposal, not finished infrastructure. Hormuz previously carried nearly 20 million bpd of oil. The IEA estimates today’s genuinely available bypass capacity at only 3.5–5.5 million bpd. Diverting 50–70% would require roughly 10–14 million bpd, plus new pumping stations, storage tanks and export terminals. The biggest flaw is LNG: Qatar ships around 9.3 billion cubic feet per day through Hormuz. LNG cannot simply be pumped through an oil pipeline. A replacement would require enormous gas pipelines across several countries or entirely new liquefaction and export terminals outside the Gulf. Reducing dependence on Hormuz is possible. Making it irrelevant by 2028 is not a construction plan yet. It is a political prediction with a very large engineering gap.

The Makkah Joint Defense Agreement enables the three signatory countries to develop joint defense capabilities, strengthen strategic deterrence, enhance readiness, and further develop and integrate their respective defense capabilities to jointly address any threats to their safety and security. Under the agreement, any external armed attack against any one of the three countries shall be regarded as an attack against all three. The agreement does not represent an effort to establish a military axis or a sectarian bloc. Nor is it linked to any nuclear ambitions or arms race, rather it is focused on building sustainable capabilities. The agreement does not come at the expense of the Kingdom’s strong and strategic relations with its Gulf, Arab, and international partners. It does not constitute a threat to the security of any country in the region, nor does it represent an escalation of tensions between any two states. The agreement does not supersede or replace any existing bilateral or multilateral agreements between these countries, or between them and other states or international organizations.
